source: Wu, Li, Tafjord, Kim (2026) XYEval: Agents say yes to bad advice
finding: Closest direct test of a wrong supplied cause on coding agents. A plausible but wrong suggestion (wrong file, wrong code change, or wrong root-cause analysis) was injected into SWE-bench Verified issue text. Pass@1 fell for all three Gemini models.
numbers: SWE-bench Verified pass@1, original to wrong-suggestion: Gemini 3.1 Pro 77.2 to 68.8; Gemini 3.5 Flash 78.0 to 70.8; Gemini 3.7 Flash 79.8 to 71.4. That is a relative drop of about 9 to 11%. Terminal-Bench drops reached 46.7% relative. Five models, six benchmarks; one SWE-bench Pro cell rose 2.4% (Gemini 3.7 Flash).
quote: Agents suffer large XY drops under XY mutation across benchmarks, with relative drops reaching up to 46.7%
limits: The wrong suggestion came from a user, not from the agent's own hypothesis. No correct-hint arm and no equal-token control. Drop is smaller on SWE-bench than on interactive tasks because agents can run tests.
agent_relevance: Gap 2 is partly closed: a wrong supplied cause does cost a modest but real share of repairs. Our test should add the correct-hint arm and equal tokens. Claude Opus 4.8 was the most resistant model, so size depends on the model.

source: Wu et al. (2026) XYEval, comply-instruction and trace analyses
finding: Even when told to follow the wrong suggestion exactly, agents still solved many tasks by running tests. Wrong advice did not make traces longer. The harm shows up as off-track reasoning, not as more turns.
numbers: SWE-bench Verified pass@1 with comply instruction: Gemini 3.1 Pro 50.2 (orig 77.2, XY 68.8); Gemini 3.5 Flash 60.6 (orig 78.0, XY 70.8). Average turn counts nearly identical under XY and control (Figure 4).
quote: even under explicit system instructions to always follow misleading suggestions, agents still solve 50.2%-60.6% of tasks
limits: Only Gemini models in this table. Turn count is a weak proxy for tokens; token counts are not given.
agent_relevance: Real execution feedback is the main defence against a wrong hypothesis (supports K09). The cost of anchoring is not in length, so a token budget alone will not detect fixation. Track which hypothesis the agent is testing instead.

source: Wu et al. (2026) XYEval, mitigation prompts
finding: A general warning about misleading advice only partly helps on SWE-bench. Naming the exact wrong suggestion (an oracle) restores the original score.
numbers: SWE-bench Verified relative drop, no defence / generic XY warning / oracle (golden) defence: Gemini 3.1 Pro -10.9% / -11.1% / +1.3%; 3.5 Flash -9.2% / -6.7% / -0.8%; 3.7 Flash -10.5% / -9.3% / -7.9%. Terminal-Bench: the warning cut a -46.7% drop to -18.3% for 3.1 Pro.
limits: The generic warning is a prompt, not a protocol. The oracle defence is an upper bound, not usable.
agent_relevance: A rule like 'distrust supplied causes' is not enough. The agent needs a check that can reject a supplied hypothesis, such as a prediction that is run. Test this against a plain warning.

source: Verma (2026) Try Again, Don't Look Back: Blind Resampling Outperforms Self-Repair in Small Code Models
finding: Pre-registered, matched-budget test on MBPP+. Showing the model its own failed program hurt compared with a fresh draw from the original prompt, up to 3B. At 7B the arms tied. Execution feedback added nothing over a content-free 'wrong' notice.
numbers: pass@1 at k=8 (resample / placebo / feedback / reflect) and output tokens: 1.5B .749 / .688 / .688 / .688, 63k / 90k / 129k / 345k; 3B .778 / .709 / .735 / .743, 76k / 89k / 84k / 284k; 7B .820 / .802 / .810 / .828, 49k / 59k / 55k / 122k. placebo minus resample = -0.061 (p=0.006) at 1.5B and -0.069 (p<0.001) at 3B. Near-identical retries: 33 to 68% vs 2 to 14%. About half of attainable gain arrives by k=2.
quote: Showing a model its own failed program makes it less likely to succeed than simply asking again
limits: Qwen2.5-Coder 1.5B/3B/7B Q4 plus one DeepSeek replication, MBPP+ function-level tasks only, a single-author preprint. No frontier models, no multi-file bugs.
agent_relevance: Gap 10 gets a first partial answer: for small models, restarting from the original prompt beats keeping the failed attempt. For frontier models it is untested. The mechanism is anchoring on the model's own earlier answer, the LLM form of fixation (supports K07, K14).

source: Verma (2026) Blind Resampling, anchoring and cross-task controls
finding: The harm is specific to conditioning on the model's own failed attempt. Adding solutions to other tasks changes nothing, so it is not just a longer prompt. Verbal reflection weakens the anchor but costs 2.5 to 5.5 times the tokens. The penalty size tracks baseline quality (r=0.96 across six configurations).
numbers: Cross-task retrieved solutions: effect bounded within 3.5 points. Reflection reduces similarity to the prior attempt by 0.04 to 0.12 vs feedback. At 7B reflection gains +0.8 points (not significant) for 2.5x tokens.
limits: Similarity is a text metric. The result is confounded with model size, which drives both baseline quality and anchor cost.
agent_relevance: Suggests a restart rule: after a failed hypothesis test, pass only a short list of rejected hypotheses, not the failed patch. Not yet tested against keeping full history on strong models.

source: Can (2026) Falsification, Not Exposure: placebo-controlled decomposition of self-repair feedback
finding: Preregistered test on dead tasks (no best-of-8 sample passed). Blind resampling beat bare-code retry. Executed facts added to the code beat the same code with a generic placebo. This partly conflicts with Verma on whether feedback content matters.
numbers: Three 0.5B to 1.5B models, 290 dead task-cell units, 7,000 fresh generations. Blind resampling beat bare-code retry by +18 net unlocks (discordant 25/7, Holm p=0.0021). Code plus facts beat bare code by +18 (21/3, p=0.00042) and beat generic-bullet placebo by +15 (p=0.0041). Instruction-only effect +3, p=0.36.
limits: Tiny models only. 'Dead' tasks are a selected hard subset. Preprint, single author.
agent_relevance: The two small-model papers agree that re-showing the failed code hurts, and disagree on feedback content. Our restart test should include a rejected-hypotheses-plus-observed-facts arm.

source: Arimbur (2026) How Many Tries Does It Take? Iterative Self-Repair across Model Scales
finding: Seven modern models (Llama 3.1 8B to Gemini 2.5 Pro) all improved with up to five rounds of error feedback. Most of the gain came in the first two rounds. Assertion (logic) errors were hardest to repair.
numbers: Pass-rate gain from self-repair: +4.9 to +17.1 pp on HumanEval (164 tasks) and +16.0 to +30.0 pp on MBPP Sanitized (257). Gemini 2.5 Flash final 96.3% HumanEval and 93.8% MBPP. Assertion errors repaired about 45%.
limits: No blind-resampling control at equal tokens, so it cannot separate feedback from extra draws. This is the weakness Verma names. Single-function tasks. Independent-researcher preprint. I read the abstract and opening only.
agent_relevance: Does not answer gap 3. Gains from a repair loop must be compared with best-of-N at equal output tokens. Cap repair loops at about 2 rounds.

source: Olausson et al. (2024) Is Self-Repair a Silver Bullet for Code Generation? (ICLR 2024)
finding: Equal-budget comparison with i.i.d. sampling (budget counted in tokens). Self-repair often equals or trails plain sampling at small budgets. Better feedback is what unlocks repair gains: boosted feedback beat both i.i.d. and ordinary self-repair at all budgets.
numbers: One reported cell: 1.05x the pass rate of pass@20 for one setting, and 0.97x of pass@22 when 2 initial samples and 10 repairs each were used. Stronger-model feedback given to a weaker model beat both baselines at all budgets.
limits: 2023-era GPT-3.5, GPT-4 and Code Llama on HumanEval and APPS. Not agentic, no tool use.
agent_relevance: Anchors gap 3 for older models: the repair loop is only worth its tokens when the diagnosis step is good. Our agent should compare its debug loop with best-of-N at the same token count.

finding: Replacing GPT-4's own explanation of a bug with a human one raised the repair success rate. Model explanations were much more often wrong.
numbers: 16 participants (15 graduate students, 1 professional), 40 failing GPT-4 programs, 2 human feedback strings each, 25 repair samples per feedback. Success: GPT-4 own feedback 33.30% vs human 52.60% (1.58x). By difficulty, GPT-4/human: introductory 42.64/62.21, interview 19.33/45.67, competition 3.67/14.67. Obviously wrong feedback: GPT-4 32/80, human 7/80. Humans voiced uncertainty 7/80, GPT-4 0/80.
limits: Human participants wrote feedback with no time limit; 40 programs; competitive-programming style tasks.
agent_relevance: Gap 4 stays open: the human diagnosis gap is real, but Olausson never tested generate-many-then-pick. The 0/80 uncertainty figure says the model does not mark its guesses as guesses; ask for a confidence per hypothesis.

source: Kang, Chen, Yoo, Lee (2023) Explainable Automated Debugging via LLM-driven Scientific Debugging (AutoSD), re-read
finding: Re-read for cost and for harm. AutoSD took about five times longer than the plain LLM baseline. In the 20-person patch-review study, explanations helped in most tasks, but in one task incorrect reviewers accepted AutoSD's wrong reasoning without scrutiny.
numbers: Human study: 20 participants (6 professionals, 14 students), 12 sampled bugs. Participants more accurate with explanations in 7 cases (5 on BugsInPy), less accurate in 2 (ARHE105, BIP003) at about equal review time. In BIP003 respondents became more cautious; in ARHE105 they accepted wrong reasoning. 70% wanted explanations.
quote: AutoSD could take about five times longer to generate a patch when compared to LLM-Base
limits: Method-level fault localisation was given. No equal-token best-of-N arm. Old models (Codex-era, ChatGPT).
agent_relevance: Gap 3 stays open. A fluent wrong explanation is a hazard to the reader and probably to the agent's later steps. Keep explanations paired with executed evidence.

source: Samir and Rahman (2026) CogniGent: bug localization with hypothesis and dynamic cognition (ICPC 2026)
finding: Multi-agent bug-localization pipeline that generates hypotheses and tests them by exploring the call graph. Hypothesis generation and investigation were among the components whose removal cost the most.
numbers: 591 bug reports, three open models (Devstral best). Full system MAP 0.407 document, 0.226 method. Without hypothesis module 0.379 / 0.195 (about -7% / -14%). Without investigation 0.360 / 0.183 (-11.6% / -19.0%). Without filtering 0.364 / 0.189. Full system beats the best baseline by MAP 23.33 to 38.57% (document and method).
limits: Localization only, not repair. No token or cost match, no random-hypothesis control. Ablation on one model. Authors' own method.
agent_relevance: Weak support that a hypothesis step helps localization at an unmatched cost. Hypothesis count was not varied, so gap 5 is untouched.

source: Anonymous authors (2026) SWE-Doctor: runtime diagnosis from bug reproduction tests
finding: A diagnose-then-patch agent that runs reproduction tests and records suspected fault location, symptoms and runtime values beat mini-SWE-agent and live-SWE-agent across 10 model-benchmark pairs. Removing the diagnosis stage lost 8 points on the ablation sample.
numbers: Headline resolve rate: 75.7% SWE-bench Verified, 59.4% Pro. On issues where the generated test fails before and passes after the fix (FP issues): Verified 81.4 vs 78.9 for mini-SWE-agent, Pro 65.4 vs 57.1. Ablation on 50 Pro issues, GPT-5.4-mini: full 56.0, without diagnosis stage 48.0, mini-SWE-agent 44.0, live-SWE-agent 40.0. Five-run average 54.0 (SD 2.0) vs 42.4 (SD 2.2) and 45.2 (SD 3.4). Cost per issue $0.43 vs $0.23 and $0.22 on Verified; $0.64 vs $0.52 and $0.40 on Pro.
limits: Cost is up to 2x the baseline and there is no best-of-N arm at the same cost. Ablation is 50 issues of one benchmark with one small model. The paper cites Alaboudi but does not supply hypotheses.
agent_relevance: Best current SWE-bench-style sign that an explicit diagnosis stage pays, but the equal-token control that gap 3 asks for is still missing. Report per-issue dollars next to resolve rate.

source: Alaboudi and LaToza (2020) Using Hypotheses as a Debugging Aid (VL/HCC), re-read for numbers
finding: Re-read Tables III and IV. The headline is an ordinal-regression odds ratio on 60 sessions; raw success is far less dramatic and time was not reduced.
numbers: Success per task (3 tasks, 20 sessions per condition): control 4/8, 2/6, 5/6 = 11/20; fault locations 2/6, 4/6, 7/8 = 13/20; potential hypotheses 5/6, 5/8, 6/6 = 16/20. Odds ratio 6.24, SE 0.88, p=0.03; fault locations 1.4 (p=0.64); years of experience 1.14 (p=0.04); technology knowledge 2.19 (p=0.07). Time: f=0.51, p=0.61. My calculation, taking SE as log-scale: 95% CI about 1.1 to 35. My Fisher exact test on 16/20 vs 11/20: p about 0.18; vs 24/40 for the other two groups: p about 0.15. Control group hypotheses: 27, 35, 38 across stages with 3, 9, 15 correct (11, 25, 39%); median 1 per participant in stages 1 and 2, 2 in stage 3. Fault locations vs control: correct hypotheses p=0.41 (stage 2), p=0.13 (stage 3); fix rate p=0.67.
quote: participants who received potential debugging hypotheses were six times more likely to fix the fault
limits: Both supplied arms included one correct and one wrong item (for locations the wrong one was listed first), so wrong-only was never run. Simple web bugs from Stack Overflow, Internet blocked, mostly students. Participants enumerated hypotheses before testing, which is not natural practice.
agent_relevance: Gap 6 is not closed: the effect is a wide-interval odds ratio from N=20 per arm. A wrong item was always present beside a right one, so wrong-only fixation is unmeasured in humans too.

source: Huang, Mustafin, Piccioni, Schena, Weber, Meyer (2025) Do AI models help produce verified bug fixes?
finding: Randomised human study with a formal prover as the judge. The group with LLM access did not solve more bugs than the group without. The authors saw 'hallucination loops': the LLM guessed a wrong fix, the programmer tried it, it failed to verify, and they looped without understanding the cause. Collaborator-style users did best.
numbers: 24 screen recordings in two groups, 9 Eiffel/AutoProof tasks, GPT-4o mini through a chat site. In the solved-task chart all indications (minima, maxima, medians) were lower for the LLM group; the authors call this coarse and give no test. Copy-paster style was common (38%) but low-yield.
quote: The AI tool makes an incorrect guess about how to correct a bug; the programmer tries it, the result does not verify
limits: Small N, no significance test on the headline, one language, one weak model. Other percentages for user types are garbled in my text extract and not recorded.
agent_relevance: Human parallel to LLM fixation: a wrong supplied cause traps the user. Supports an agent rule: when a fix fails to verify twice, return to hypothesis generation and do not patch the patch.

source: Bertolazzi, Tentori, Bernardi (2026) FalsifyBench: rule-discovery games for LLMs
finding: Twelve LLMs played Wason 2-4-6 style hidden-property games. Negative testing (seeking to falsify) was the main driver of success. The paper restates Klayman and Ha: negative tests are needed only when the hypothesis is narrower than the true rule; when it is broader, positive tests can falsify it.
numbers: 12 LLMs; reasoning models stronger than instruction-tuned; no model near optimal. No code or debugging task in the paper.
quote: The primary driver of success is the capacity for negative testing
limits: Semantic category games, not programs. Does not test the Think-in-Opposites or Dual-Goal prompts. Prompt-intervention numbers were not found in my reading.
agent_relevance: Gap 9 stays open. The Klayman-Ha condition gives a code-specific test: a guess naming a too-narrow cause (one input path) needs a disconfirming run outside it; a too-broad guess can be falsified by a positive run. Choose by hypothesis scope, not 'always disconfirm'.

source: Biolo, Tezza, Gong, Massacci (2026) Helpful or Harmful? LLM-assisted vulnerability patching, registered report; related-work passage on Serafini et al.
finding: This paper is a protocol with a pilot and no results. Its related-work section reports that a deliberately manipulated ChatGPT recommending insecure MD5 produced over-reliance that neither warnings nor prompt interventions removed (Serafini et al., N=76). Seen only second-hand.
numbers: Serafini et al. N=76 as cited. Perry et al. N=47: less secure code on 4 of 5 tasks while rating it more secure. Steenhoek et al., 17 professionals: 18% of alerts and 25% of LLM fixes useful without significant problems.
limits: Second-hand summary; the primary study was not opened. Security patching, not general debugging.
agent_relevance: Human evidence that warnings do not stop adoption of a wrong supplied suggestion, matching the XYEval warning result. Not a primary source for our claims.
